extracted.intended_audience: students and aspiring public relations practitioners; practicing PR professionals and educators
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-level framework describing the definition, functions, models, ethics, and knowledge base for professional public relations practice, aimed at teaching research, planning, evaluation, and communication-management skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as management of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is the management of communication between an organization and its publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR professionals manage movement of messages into and out of the organization, conduct research on publics, counsel management on organizational policies/actions, and plan and execute communications (e.g., write news stories or fact sheets) so organizational decisions are explained to publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on management role
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should be treated as part of the management subsystem rather than mere publicity or pleasant social behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR is expected to help top management plan and evaluate total communication activities, control conflict among subsystems, and integrate organizational responses to environmental demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social and behavioral science (communication science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practice should be based on knowledge from the social and behavioral sciences, especially communication research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students need focused exposure to relevant social science concepts (communication science, psychology, sociology, political science, etc.) rather than indiscriminate 'information overload.' Practitioners should keep up with new ideas in communication research and apply them to PR problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of theory and technical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A true professional integrates a conceptual framework (theory) with technical communication skills (practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conceptual framework should indicate when and how to use technical skills to solve PR problems; the book aims to provide both conceptual understanding and a set of technical skills for research, planning, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of a body of knowledge and technical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations professionals should possess a distinct body of knowledge and have mastered communication techniques not known by the average citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalization implies formal training and mastery comparable in concept (if not in form) to other professions like law or medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics and values
rubrics_metrics.description: PR professionals must have a set of values and a code of ethics that discourage use of knowledge and technical skills for antisocial or harmful purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics help prevent misuse (e.g., assisting antisocial groups); professionalization, not restriction or banning, is the solution to unethical uses of PR techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek professional status and formal training
rubrics_metrics.description: The field should professionalize—moving beyond roots in press agentry and propaganda by developing formal training and a common body of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many practitioners historically came from journalism/advertising with little formal PR education, establishing curricula and social-science grounding is recommended to raise standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way communication and mutual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective public relations emphasizes two-way communication (especially the two-way symmetric model) to achieve mutual understanding between organization and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and models that stress mutual understanding suggest PR activity should adapt both organization to environment and environment to organization, and may involve persuading management as well as publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of multiple possible effects (persuasion, understanding, communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations may aim at persuasion, mutual understanding, or merely communication; definitions should not limit PR to a single desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different practitioners and activities may prioritize different effects—evaluative criteria should therefore accommodate persuasion, information, and relationship-building outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four models of public relations practice
rubrics_metrics.description: PR practice can be categorized into four models—press agent/publicity, public-information, two-way asymmetric, and two-way symmetric—each with different objectives, settings, means, and evaluation methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the model taxonomy to understand historical stages and to choose appropriate objectives and evaluation measures; recognize many organizations/practitioners operate in earlier models rather than the full managerial model.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR as an organizational subsystem and boundary role
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations functions as a subsystem that operates at organizational boundaries—liaising between the organization and external groups while having one foot inside and one outside the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As boundary personnel, PR supports other subsystems (production, disposal, maintenance, adaptive, management) by communicating across boundaries and bringing external ideas in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support of organizational subsystems (production, disposal, maintenance, adaptive, management)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR should support production/disposal (marketing and distribution), maintenance (personnel/employee development), adaptive (research and planning), and management subsystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PR can promote products (disposal subsystem), support employee communication (maintenance), bring new ideas into the organization (adaptive), and counsel management on communication strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core PR activities: research, planning, evaluation, counseling, writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners should engage in research on publics, plan programs, evaluate outcomes, counsel management, and produce communication materials (press releases, fact sheets, speeches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities form the technical skills PR students must learn and the practical tools used to solve PR problems across organizational sizes and settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness and feedback to management
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations increases organizational responsiveness by channeling feedback from publics to management and helping management adapt policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR acts as an early warning system to anticipate trends and to advise management so decisions consider public opinion and environmental changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve the public interest and provide an articulate public voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners serve the public interest by providing a clear, articulate voice in the public forum for ideas, individuals, and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR increases public knowledge by delivering information through media that may lack the resources to provide it themselves; serving public interest is part of professional responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unethical/irresponsible tactics (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should avoid tactics that 'choke channels of communication with the debris of pseudo-events,' cloud or conceal facts, or otherwise produce cynicism and distrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cutlip's listed 'minuses' of PR include: overuse of pseudo-events, concealment of facts, and contributing to public cynicism—these are explicit anti-patterns to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep up with communication research and evolving knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must pay attention to and maintain currency with communication research developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although communication research has progressed, practitioners often lag; continual learning ensures PR methods are informed by the latest social-science findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different evaluation methods for different PR models
rubrics_metrics.description: Because PR models have different objectives, they 'generally require different means of evaluating their success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select evaluation criteria appropriate to the model in use (e.g., publicity impressions vs. mutual understanding vs. behavior change) rather than a one-size-fits-all metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include irresponsible or ineffective practices within the definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of public relations should not exclude ineffective or irresponsible practices; those activities are still PR even if they fail professional standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to medicine or law, failure or unethical practice does not mean the activity isn't public relations; definitions should be broad enough to encompass varied quality and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional education should be focused (avoid information overload)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR education should give focused exposure to social-science concepts relevant to PR problems rather than overwhelming students with unrelated material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula that draw from appropriate subdisciplines (e.g., social psychology, organizational behavior) and emphasize application to research, planning, and evaluation.
